newsitem.title: USA: US West unit's mega debt deal meets mega demand.
newsitem.headline: US West unit's mega debt deal meets mega demand.

text.p: US West Capital Funding's $4.1 billion multi-tranche debt offering met with huge demand and was oversubsribed going into the pricing, market players said.
"The deal was a blowout and came in on the tighter side of price talk," said one high-grade syndicate source.
Another player echoed this view, "It was a huge success and is issue-bid on the street."
The issue by the unit of US West Inc grabbed the title of largest investment grade deal ever priced in U.S. corporate bond history.
Until then, Lockheed Martin Corp's $3.5 billion debt offering in May, 1996 held the record, according to research firm, Securities Data Co.
The size of the deal was boosted three times to more than double the $2.0 billion initially planned, but players were still scrambling to get a piece of the offering.
"Investors were searching for yield and then there was this BBB-rated deal and demand skyrocketed," another syndicate source said.
Dealers said on Thursday that the six-tranche debt offering was priced as follows:
-$600 million 6.85 percent five-year notes priced to yield 55 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
-$1.1 billion 7.30 percent 10-year notes priced to yield 80 basis points over Treasuries.
-$1.1 bllion 7.90 percent 30-year debt priced to yield 107 basis points over Treasuries.
-$600 million 6.95 percent 40-year bonds priced to yield 56 basis points over Treasuries and is puttable in the seventh year.
-$500 million 7.95 percent 100-year bonds priced to yield 120 basis points over Treasuries.
-$200 million in 8.15 percent 35-year bonds priced to yield 132 basis points over Treasuries.
Securities Data noted that while the US West Capital deal was the largest investment-grade debt deal ever, it also tied the overall record for largest corporate debt offering of any type.
Not since RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp's $4.1 billion junk bond deal had the market seen a debt offering of such proportion.

Merrill Lynch & Co, which served as lead underwriter on the $4.1 billion multi-tranche debt offering, said the deal was significantly oversubscribed and could have been sold in excess of $5.0 billion.

"It was issue-bid going into the pricing even after growing the deal it was significantly oversubscribed...we could have easily priced it in excess of $5.0 billion," said Jack Weingart, managing director at Merrill Lynch Capital Markets Group.

The lead manager said the deal was initially begun as a $2.0 billion four-part debt offering but was met with such huge demand that various tranches were upped in size and two new issues, a century bond and 35-year bond, had to be added.
"We worked with the company to ensure that we were growing each tranche in response to investor demand," Weingart said. "The 10- and 30-year were the most oversubscribed tranches."
Both tranches were upped in size to $1.1 billion from $500 million, the underwriter said.
According to Merrill Lynch, all proceeds from the deal will be used to pay down commercial paper.
